Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

rTFT 0.2.1

Bug fixes

  • loo_hazard() stopped with “argument is not interpretable as logical” when loo could not estimate the Pareto k of a unit, as loo 2.10.0 cannot for a fit whose chains did not mix. On a cluster the fit was then lost with its task. Such a unit is now counted among those for which PSIS cannot be trusted, in the warning of loo_hazard() and in high_k of the summary that fit_hazard_models() and collect_hpc() return.

rTFT 0.2.0

Comparing and averaging models

  • build_hazard_models() builds a table of models to compare, one row for each failure-rate function with a baseline and the formulas of its parameters. A formula is given to the models that have its parameter, and a name that is misspelt is reported before anything is fitted.
  • fit_hazard_models() fits every model of the table to the same data, checks the sampling of each fit by one rule (Rhat, the effective sample sizes and the divergent transitions, met or not in the column rule_met of its summary), and cross-validates each with the same unit left out, by importance sampling and, when asked, by refitting with the same folds for every model. A model that fails does not stop the others. It returns the fits and the cross-validation results as hazard_weights() and the average_*() functions read them, with a summary of one row per model.
  • hazard_weights() names a model that gives some unit left out no chance at all (a log predictive density of -Inf), as a model with a threshold can for a unit whose failures it places below the threshold. Pseudo-BMA gives such a model a weight of zero; stacking can still weight it, even the most, when other models predict that unit, and the message and the help say why. A unit that no model gives any chance stops the weighting with an error that names it, where the stacking would otherwise fail without saying why.

Running on a cluster

  • write_hpc_bundle() writes a table of models, its data and the settings of the run into one folder, to be copied to a cluster that schedules its jobs with Slurm, with scripts written for the clusters of the Digital Research Alliance of Canada. The run is checked, the unit left out in cross-validation chosen and the folds assigned before anything is written, and the account, time, memory and modules are written once, in the folder’s settings.sh.
  • check_hpc_bundle(), run on the cluster by the folder’s check.sh, checks by their checksums that the files arrived unchanged, that the installed rTFT is the version that wrote them (and, between releases, from the same commit), that cmdstanr finds CmdStan, and that every model can be assembled, before anything is submitted.
  • run_hpc_task() runs one task of a bundle on the cluster: it fits one model, as fit_hazard_models() fits it, or refits one model without the units of one fold, starting from the model’s fit. A task whose result is already there is not run again, and each task records how it ended, with the reason for a failure. When the bundle was written with a seed, each refit seeds R from it and from the task’s number, so that the effects it draws for the units left out, and so its estimate, are the same when it is run again.
  • The bundle’s submit.sh submits the fits as one job array and the refits for cross-validation as another, queued to start when the fits have ended, and task.sh runs each task. A task that failed or ran out of time can be submitted again alone.
  • hpc_status(), run on the cluster by the bundle’s status.sh, says what each task has done and why a task is not done, including a task that Slurm stopped (out of time, out of memory, or for a reason of its own), and gives the command that submits again only the tasks not done, leaving out those still waiting in the queue or running.
  • collect_hpc() assembles the results, once they have been copied back, into what fit_hazard_models() returns. Each result carries the checksums of the bundle it was computed from, so it is never assembled with another; models and folds without a result are named.
  • next_hpc_round() writes the next round of a bundle for some of its models, typically those that did not converge, with new settings of the sampler and of the jobs. The data, the unit, the folds and the sampling rule are copied from the bundle, never chosen again, as are the place on the cluster the bundle is copied to and where rTFT is installed from, and a change that would make another model, such as a prior, is refused. A round can name any model of the first bundle, so a model left out of one round can be fitted again in a later one. collect_hpc(), given the folders of a bundle and of its rounds, takes each model from its latest round, even when that round failed or has no result yet, and says which round in a new column of the summary, round.
  • The bundle’s folder inputs/ holds the data, the models, the settings and the tasks with their checksums; write_hpc_bundle() refuses a table in which the same model appears under two names, which would be weighted twice; each model is compiled into a folder of its own under stan/, so that two models with the same Stan code are never compiled into one file at the same time; and install.sh keeps its temporary files out of the login node’s /tmp, which is small and shared.
  • A fifth vignette, Fitting models on a cluster, takes a user who has never used a cluster from an account on the clusters of the Digital Research Alliance of Canada to the assembled results of a comparison, with the output of real runs on the Fir cluster.

Checking a fitted model

  • hazard_residuals() draws the residuals several times with n_randomisations, so that a pattern can be told apart from the luck of one draw. Under the same seed the first randomisation is the one a single draw gives. The output gains a column, randomisation. The help says how far each kind of residual can move between draws: not at all for a failure at a known time, within its interval for a failure known to an interval, and up to 1 for a survivor.
  • plot_residuals() draws several randomisations faintly, against the uniform distribution as a line each.
  • check_survival() warns when a group holds fewer than five individuals, as every group does when each individual has a temperature trajectory of its own. In a group that small the band of simulated proportions is wide, often from 0 to 1, and a model wrong for every individual can pass; the residuals, which pool every individual, are then the check to judge by.

Bug fixes

  • A failure-rate function or a baseline given as a factor was read by its position among the factor’s levels, not by its text, so another function of the catalogue could be fitted without an error. fit_hazard() and the other functions that take m_form or baseline now refuse anything but a single character string.
  • loo_hazard(), and fit_hazard_models() through it, could hang for good where the option mc.cores was set above 1, as is common with brms: the loo package then copied the R process to work on several cores, and a copy made once a sampler’s threads were running could wait forever. It now asks the loo package for one core; a matrix of one column per unit is quick on one.
  • A temperature path with two readings at one time, as when a sudden change is written as two readings at the moment of the change, was accepted: build_hazard_data() replaced the two by their mean and followed a path that climbed steadily instead of jumping, with only a warning from base R. A path must now have one reading at each time, and a sudden change is written as two readings a moment apart.
  • Where a temperature path bends within an interval at risk (a logged record, or a ramp held and then resumed, checked less often than it was logged), build_hazard_data() cut the interval into equal parts sized from its whole span, so the parts over the steep stretch could change by more than grid_dT, by over a degree in an example with a short steep climb. A part that still changes by more than grid_dT is now cut again. Paths that are straight between checks, such as those of the vignettes, give the same table as before.

Other changes

  • The estimate by refitting is no longer called exact. The effect of each unit left out is drawn at random, so two runs without a seed give different estimates (they differed by about 1 in elpd in a test on a cluster), and a seed gives the same estimate again without making it more precise. The help of kfold_hazard() and fit_hazard_models() says so, and the help of fit_hazard_models() says where the limits of its sampling rule come from.
  • tools is imported (for the checksums of a bundle), cmdstanr and withr are suggested, and Additional_repositories names the repository of cmdstanr, which is not on CRAN.
  • The help of build_hazard_data() says what the default time grid costs at a high thermal sensitivity (about 1% in b at b = 4.7, from simulations), and advises a step of 0.05 where b is above about 3. Its warning for a failure interval that spans more than half a degree now says how large the bias can be on a ramp checked at long intervals (b 20% low at b = 4.7 with intervals of up to 0.9 degrees), and the help advises checking more often.

rTFT 0.1.1

Bug fixes

  • From version 2.10.0, loo::loo_compare() gives the compared models in a column rather than as row names. A test and the vignette “Comparing and averaging models” read the row names; both now read the models from either place. The functions of the package are unchanged.

Other changes

  • The package has a DOI, given by citation("rTFT") and the README.
  • The package is checked on Linux, macOS and Windows with each push.
  • The package can be installed from R-universe.
  • The website has a page title and description for search engines.

rTFT 0.1.0

First release.

Fitting

  • build_hazard_data() builds the table of intervals at risk from failure times that are known-time, interval-censored or a mixture of both, under any temperature trajectory. ramp_path() builds the trajectory of a linear ramp, and assess_ramp_linearity() compares a logged ramp with a straight line.
  • fit_hazard() fits the model using Bayesian inference in Stan through brms, with a choice of functions for the failure rate (M_catalogue) and for the baseline (h0_catalogue). The failure rate may depend on covariates and on group-level effects.
  • costressor() declares a co-stressor (e.g., dissolved oxygen), with its main effect and, when asked for, its interaction with temperature. A model may have more than one co-stressor.
  • build_hazard_prior() shows and sets the priors.

Checking a fitted model

  • check_survival() and plot_check() compare the proportion of individuals observed to survive with the proportions simulated from the model.
  • hazard_residuals() and plot_residuals() give one randomised residual per individual.

Derived quantities

  • derive_tdt_ttl() derives the static critical thermal maximum, the thermal death time curves and the thermal tolerance landscape, and derive_dctmax() the dynamic critical thermal maximum under a ramp, each with its posterior uncertainty.
  • plot_tdt(), plot_ttl() and plot_ttl_3d() draw them.
  • M_draws() returns the posterior draws of the failure rate across temperatures.

Comparing and averaging models

  • loo_hazard() and kfold_hazard() compare models by cross-validation that leaves out whole individuals or trials.
  • hazard_weights() gives the weights of the models, and average_tdt_ttl(), average_dctmax() and average_survival() average the derived quantities and the predictions.

Predicting survival

  • predict_survival() predicts survival along a record of temperature (and of any co-stressors recorded with it), and reports how much of the record and of the predicted risk lies outside the temperatures and exposure times of the assay. plot_survival() and plot_risk() draw the prediction.

Data

  • static_assay, ramp_assay and stream_record are simulated datasets used in the help pages and the vignettes.
